scoreRule: 1 point per correct MC item; 10 points maximum; local provisional grade only
description: Ten newly written comprehension, interpretation and situational transfer questions; pending independent teacher review.

questions.q: What made the challenge a genuine change in communication?
choices: It banned chats while still allowing calls and email.
It required pupils to stop speaking for a week.
It made all phones unusable after school.
It prevented every form of online learning.
questions.explanation: The experiment targets messaging habits, not all communication or phone use.

questions.q: What does the writer's repeated phone-checking reveal?
choices: He is expecting an emergency call from his coach.
He has developed a strong habit of looking for messages.
His phone displays forty new messages before lunch.
His teacher asks him to monitor group chats.
questions.explanation: He keeps checking despite knowing there can be no new chats.

questions.q: What surprised Karim about the telephone call?
choices: He had forgotten the time of the football practice.
He could not recognize the writer's voice.
He thought a call might mean something serious had happened.
He expected the call to last twenty minutes.
questions.explanation: Karim's reaction shows how unusual a simple call has become.

questions.q: Why does the writer compare a short call with many chat messages?
choices: He concludes that sending text is never useful.
He wants everyone to stop discussing football.
He believes calls take longer than group chats.
He discovers that some practical questions are resolved faster by speaking.
questions.explanation: The call gives a direct answer without the usual lengthy group discussion.

questions.q: What weakness of relying on chats does the history-group incident reveal?
choices: Group meetings must always happen in the library.
Important changes may not reach somebody who is temporarily offline.
The writer has forgotten how to send an email.
Teachers should not assign group presentations.
questions.explanation: The group changes the meeting place, and the writer only learns too late.

questions.q: Why does the writer keep the apps but change their settings?
choices: The teacher orders the whole class to delete messages.
His friends will never speak on the phone.
The challenge proves every messaging service is unsafe.
He wants more control rather than a complete ban.
questions.explanation: He resumes messaging while switching off unnecessary notifications.

questions.q: A student needs one quick answer from a teammate. Which solution fits the experiment?
choices: Make a short call instead of starting a long group discussion.
Send the same question twenty times in the chat.
Wait until every group member writes a reply.
Avoid asking because a call seems unusual.
questions.explanation: The writer's call to Karim provides a model for direct communication.

questions.q: A project group changes the meeting room at short notice. What would help an offline member?
choices: Assume everyone reads the group chat immediately.
Never change any plan even when necessary.
Use an agreed alternative way to share urgent updates.
Write only after the meeting has finished.
questions.explanation: The missed history meeting shows that a shared chat is not always enough.

questions.q: Someone feels they must answer every group notification immediately. What could they try?
choices: Delete every contact from their phone.
Turn off low-priority alerts and choose when to respond.
Keep checking the phone more often.
Stop speaking to people outside school.
questions.explanation: The conclusion describes selective notification settings and personal choice.

questions.q: What would be a fair summary of the writer's new attitude?
choices: Messaging apps are responsible for every problem.
Calls should replace all emails and group messages.
A week offline proves digital friendships are impossible.
Different situations need different ways to communicate.
questions.explanation: The writer keeps messaging but uses calls and notifications more deliberately.
